- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.4), model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid excessive sell-off bias.  
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., > +0.5 in sentiment or +10%+ price jump), model often overshoots downward; reduce forecast dip by 5–10% to account for mean reversion.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mildly positive (e.g., 0 to +0.3), model frequently underestimates upward momentum; add 2–5% to forecast to capture sentiment-driven rally.  
- Model consistently underpredicts true price in early 30-day horizon (especially days 1–5); apply a 3–5% upward bias for first 5 days if sentiment is positive.  
- If sentiment shows strong upward trend (e.g., > +0.3 over 3–5 days), model often fails to capture momentum; increase forecast by 3–7% for next 5–7 days.  
- Model tends to lag sentiment shifts by 2–3 days; if sentiment turns positive, delay forecast adjustment by 1–2 days to avoid premature reaction.  
- When sentiment is volatile (e.g., ±0.3 or more in 3–5 days), model overfits short-term noise; smooth forecast by averaging last 3–5 days’ values before adjustment.
